To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary fiber from whole plant foods has beneficial effects on health, and that fiber supplements are not the same as dietary fiber and cannot be presumed to have the same beneficial effects.

the clinically meaningful health benefits associated with dietary fiber in foods can only be obtained by eating fiber-rich foods, not by taking fiber supplements; that only fiber supplements that possess the physical characteristics of fiber from foods will drive clinically meaningful health benefits; and that the health benefits of fiber supplements are not the same as those of fiber from foods, and therefore cannot be presumed.

dietary fiber from whole plant foods is the most efficacious fiber for health benefits and that fiber supplements can only be presumed to be efficacious if they possess the physical characteristics (solubility/fermentability, viscosity/gel formation) that drive clinical efficacy and the mechanisms that drive the health benefits.
In summary, our research is concerned with

identifying and characterizing dietary fibers that are effective in preventing/relieving constipation and/or in improving other clinically meaningful health benefits (eg. glycemic control, weight loss, weight maintenance).
the mechanisms of clinically meaningful health benefits that are driven by specific fiber characteristics.
identifying and characterizing fiber supplements that have clinically meaningful health benefits when consumed at levels consistent with the dietary fiber intake recommendations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dietary fiber from food sources has many beneficial effects on health, but the fiber supplements that are on the market today cannot be presumed to have the same effects.
fiber supplements are not a panacea and should be viewed as a tool that can be used to improve the diet and health of consumers.
the health benefits that can be attributed to dietary fiber are not necessarily the same for isolated fiber supplements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fiber supplements are not all alike.

fiber supplements can provide clinically meaningful health benefits when they are designed to provide specific fiber characteristics that drive clinically meaningful health benefits, but they are not a substitute for dietary fiber.
the health benefits of dietary fiber are driven by 3 mechanisms (small bowel, large bowel, and systemic effects) that can be targeted with specific fiber supplements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
not all fiber supplements are the same, and the fiber source, physical characteristics, and clinically meaningful health benefits must all be understood to achieve the desired health outcomes.
the fiber source, processing, and formulation of the fiber supplement all influence the efficacy of fiber supplements.

not all fiber supplements are created equal and that fiber supplements should be selected based on the health benefits that they can provide, the mechanisms by which they work, and the fiber characteristics that drive those mechanisms.
